enrichment.short_title: Deferred MHRT discharge and section 72(3) MHA 1983
key_facts: The mother of a section 3 patient applied for permission to challenge a Mental Health Review Tribunal decision deferring discharge for five weeks to arrange aftercare.
The tribunal had not expressly linked the deferral to danger on release, though the judge considered that finding would have been open on the evidence, including past refusal to eat.
An anonymity order was made for the patient and family; the Official Solicitor was invited to act.
Only two weeks of the deferral period remained when the permission application was heard.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to apply for judicial review of a Mental Health Review Tribunal deferred-discharge decision.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; the claim was treated as academic because an effective hearing before the deferral expired was unlikely.
enrichment.ratio: Section 72(1)(b)(iii) and section 72(3) of the Mental Health Act 1983 must be read together: a tribunal may defer discharge to a future date if immediate release would likely be dangerous but proper aftercare by that date would remove the risk; that power is available on a nearest-relative application under section 3.
legal_issues: Whether section 72(3) permits deferred discharge on a nearest-relative application
Whether deferral for aftercare alone is unlawful
Whether the tribunal had sufficient evidence of danger to justify deferral
Whether the claim was academic
linked_authorities: R v On the Application of Ashworth Hospital Authority v Mental Health Review Tribunal

enrichment.short_title: Fresh asylum claim refused after late military document

statutes_considered.title: Geneva Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees

key_facts: A Ukrainian claimant who left to avoid military service had his asylum appeal dismissed in August 2001.
After leave to appeal was refused, he received a military commissariat letter dated 27 August 2001 but did not promptly send it to the Secretary of State.
His solicitors sought a fresh claim in March 2002, the day after renewed permission for judicial review was refused in earlier proceedings.
The Secretary of State refused to treat the letter as a fresh claim and certified the application under section 73(8) as having no legitimate purpose.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's refusal to accept further representations as a fresh asylum claim and of section 73(8) certification.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no extension of time granted to challenge the October 2002 decision.
enrichment.ratio: Where a late document is neither sufficiently significant nor credible to found a fresh claim, lacks provenance, and was withheld during earlier proceedings, the Secretary of State was entitled to refuse a fresh claim and to certify under section 73(8) that the application's purpose was delay rather than a legitimate asylum or Article 3 claim.
legal_issues: Whether the military commissariat letter met the criteria for a fresh claim
Lawfulness of section 73(8) certification
Whether delay in challenging the October 2002 decision should be excused
Article 3 claim based on medical exemption from military service

enrichment.short_title: Withdrawal of paragraph 9 asylum certificate after adjudicator
key_facts: A Zimbabwean claimant's asylum claim was certified under paragraph 9 of Schedule IV and dismissed by an adjudicator who agreed with the certificate.
Following the Court of Appeal decision in Zenovics, fresh evidence was submitted and the claimant appealed to the Immigration Appeal Tribunal on his human rights claim.
Keith J held the Secretary of State could and should have withdrawn the asylum certificate after Zenovics.
The IAT later dismissed the human rights appeal, rendering the case academic for the respondent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Secretary of State's appeal from a judicial review decision on power to withdraw a paragraph 9 certificate.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the Secretary of State has no power to withdraw a paragraph 9 certificate once an adjudicator has agreed with it.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 9(2) of Schedule IV to the Asylum and Immigration Act 1999 removes the right of appeal to the Immigration Appeal Tribunal once the adjudicator agrees with the Secretary of State's certificate; that bar takes effect on confirmation and is not undone by any later purported withdrawal of the certificate.
legal_issues: Whether the Secretary of State may withdraw a paragraph 9 certificate after adjudicator confirmation
Effect of partial certification after Zenovics
Construction of paragraph 9(2)
Human rights implications of fast-track certification

enrichment.short_title: Brussels Convention stay refused in defective TV coil dispute

statutes_considered.title: 1968 Brussels Convention on Jurisdiction and Enforcement of Judgments in Civil and Commercial Matters

key_facts: Sagem sued Lecerf and Miles Platt in France over defective electro-plated pins in television coils; Miles Platt sued Townroe in England for defective plating work.
A French judicial expertise process involving Miles Platt and Townroe was held not to be the court first seised for Article 21 purposes.
Townroe sought a mandatory stay under Article 21 or a discretionary stay under Article 22.
The judge removed a stay imposed by the Master; Townroe appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a High Court decision refusing to stay English proceedings under the 1968 Brussels Convention.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no stay under Article 21 or Article 22.
enrichment.ratio: A French judicial expertise process is a provisional measure under Article 24, not substantive proceedings for Article 21, and the French and English actions were not so closely connected under Article 22 as to require joint determination to avoid irreconcilable judgments.
legal_issues: Whether the French judicial expertise process amounted to proceedings first seised under Article 21
Characterisation of judicial expertise as provisional measures under Article 24
Whether French and English actions were related under Article 22
Application of the 1968 Brussels Convention rather than Brussels I Regulation

enrichment.short_title: Repudiatory breach of exclusive chemical supply agreement
key_facts: Bim Kemi and Blackburn Chemicals disputed whether a December 1993 fax created a binding 1994 exclusive supply and distribution agreement for anti-foam products.
Bim acquired Cellkem in Finland and, from 1997 to 1998, marketed its own silicone-based Tensidef and Prodex products in competition with Blackburn's BS 470.
Blackburn refused further BS 470 supplies in December 1998 after reports of competing Cellkem products.
At trial the judge found a binding 1994 contract and Blackburn in repudiatory breach; the Court of Appeal reversed on repudiation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and respondents' notice from a High Court trial on contract formation, breach, and termination.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Bim was in repudiatory breach and Blackburn was entitled to accept that breach by refusing further supplies.
enrichment.ratio: Where parties traded on the terms of the December 1993 fax, Bim/Cellkem's marketing of competing silicone defoamers to key Finnish customers was a repudiatory breach of the exclusive sourcing obligation, entitling Blackburn to terminate by refusing further supplies.
legal_issues: Whether the December 1993 fax became a binding contract
Construction of exclusivity, sourcing, and 20% market-share clauses
Whether Bim's sales of competing silicone products were repudiatory
Whether Blackburn's refusal to supply BS 470 was lawful acceptance of repudiation
linked_authorities: Barings plc v Coopers Lybrand

confidence.notes: Very long judgment with extensive fact-finding; core contract and repudiation holdings are clear but many subsidiary points were not pursued on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Issue-based patent trial costs after section 60(5)(d) win
key_facts: Stena failed in a patent action against Irish Ferries over multi-hull ferry technology but succeeded on a narrow section 60(5)(d) construction point.
The trial judge ordered Stena to pay 20% of Irish Ferries' costs and Irish Ferries to pay 80% of Stena's costs.
Irish Ferries appealed the costs order, arguing costs should follow the event on the action as a whole.
The section 60(5)(d) issue occupied only a small fraction of trial time and cost.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a trial judge's issue-based costs order after dismissal of the main patent claim and cross-appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Costs appeal dismissed; the judge's issue-based apportionment was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where a patent trial comprises a discrete legal issue on which the defendant succeeded and broader validity and infringement issues on which the claimant failed, an issue-based costs order reflecting the time and expense of each issue is a lawful exercise of discretion under CPR 44.3.
legal_issues: Whether costs should follow the event on the action as a whole
Lawfulness of an issue-based approach under CPR 44.3
Apportionment between section 60(5)(d) and validity/infringement issues
Interference with the trial judge's costs discretion

enrichment.short_title: Qualified privilege in police libel about open undetected file
key_facts: Peter Halford, an education welfare officer, was investigated after his stepson alleged assault; the CPS decided not to prosecute because of conflicting evidence.
DS Curtis told council personnel by telephone and letter that the police file remained open as an undetected crime.
Halford was suspended pending disciplinary proceedings but was later reinstated without sanction.
The judge ruled the publications were on occasions of qualified privilege and that no jury could properly find malice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claimant's appeal from a High Court order entering judgment for the defendants after rulings on qualified privilege and malice.
enrichment.ratio: Communications by a police officer to a local authority about the status of a child-protection investigation attract qualified privilege, and where the officer honestly believed the information given was true and relevant, malice cannot properly be inferred merely because the words left the claimant under suspicion.

enrichment.short_title: HRA damages for delayed Mental Health Review Tribunal hearings
key_facts: Multiple detained patients had already succeeded in establishing breaches of Article 5.4 because Mental Health Review Tribunal hearings were delayed.
This judgment determined whether damages were required under the Human Rights Act 1998 and, if so, in what amounts.
Claims were mainly for distress and frustration; some claimants also alleged loss of liberty or damage to mental health.
Modest damages were awarded to several claimants; others received no award where a declaration of breach was sufficient just satisfaction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Follow-up damages hearing after earlier judicial review findings of Article 5.4 breaches.
enrichment.outcome: Damages awarded in varying modest sums to PD, GM, JR, MK, TB, and B; no damages to KB and LB where declaratory relief sufficed; exemplary damages refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under sections 8 and 9(3) of the Human Rights Act 1998, damages for Article 5.4 delay are not automatic and must be necessary to afford just satisfaction; awards for distress may be made where compensatable injury is shown, but not for loss of a chance of discharge, and exemplary damages are prohibited.

Recoverability of damages for distress without pecuniary loss

enrichment.short_title: Robbery sentence replaced by section 37 hospital order
key_facts: The applicant pleaded guilty to robbery after smashing a post office security screen with a sledgehammer and stealing over £2,600.
He was sentenced to four and a half years' imprisonment on the basis of a psychiatric report that did not recommend hospital disposal.
Later reports diagnosed paranoid schizophrenia and showed he had been psychotic at the time of the offence but had not disclosed symptoms earlier because of delusional beliefs.
A bed at the Scott Clinic remained available for treatment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Out-of-time application for leave to appeal against sentence with fresh psychiatric evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Extension of time granted, leave granted, and appeal allowed; the custodial sentence was quashed and replaced with a section 37 hospital order.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh psychiatric evidence may be admitted on a late sentence appeal where the applicant's failure to disclose symptoms earlier was itself caused by the mental illness, and where the conditions for a section 37 hospital order are satisfied the court may substitute that disposal for an otherwise appropriate custodial sentence.
legal_issues: Admissibility of fresh evidence under section 23 Criminal Appeal Act 1968
Whether there was a reasonable explanation for failure to adduce the evidence at sentencing
Whether section 37 Mental Health Act 1983 criteria were met
Appropriateness of intervening in an otherwise proper custodial sentence

enrichment.short_title: Partnership bound by guarantee linked to consultancy agreement
key_facts: Henry Butcher & Co gave a £200,000 bank guarantee for David Hopkins's overdraft under a consultancy agreement to provide surveying and valuation services.
Four named partners signed the guarantee as partners and individuals; the document was later amended in a way initialled by only two partners.
The bank sued after Hopkins's borrowing exceeded the limit; the firm argued lack of partnership authority and that the guarantee was delivered in escrow.
The trial judge held the partnership and signing partners bound; the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a High Court judgment enforcing a partnership bank guarantee.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; HB&Co and the signing partners were held bound by the guarantee.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 5 of the Partnership Act 1890, where a guarantee is an integral part of a consultancy contract validly entered into as partnership business, a partner's execution of the guarantee binds the firm even if other partners did not sign and did not know all details, following Sandilands v Marsh.
legal_issues: Whether HB&Co had authority under the partnership deed to give the guarantee
Application of section 5 Partnership Act 1890 and Sandilands v Marsh
Whether individual signatories remained bound under clause 17
Whether the guarantee was delivered in escrow or invalidated by post-execution amendment
